Context

A logistics operator: receiving, warehousing, order picking and distribution. An operation where mistakes aren’t debated in a meeting — you see them the next morning in a truck that left wrongly loaded.

My role sat across three things that in most organisations live apart: the management system, the information systems, and shop-floor improvement. Keeping them together is what made any of them work.

The problem

A certified management system and a real operation tend to drift apart. The procedure says one thing, the operator does another, and the binder gets updated the week before the audit. When that happens, certification becomes an administrative cost that improves nothing.

The challenge wasn’t getting certified. It was certifying something people would actually use.

The three pieces

1. The tri-standard management system

Implementation and certification of ISO 9001, 14001 and 45001 as an integrated system, plus a full recertification cycle — which is the real test: keeping the system alive once the pressure of the first audit is gone.

Certification was run as a project, not as a quality task: scope, schedule, owners and milestones through to the external audit. That’s the difference between arriving on the date and arriving out of breath.

Documentation. Creating and maintaining forms, procedures and work instructions. The principle that held it together: document what someone is going to read. A work instruction nobody opens isn’t a control, it’s a liability — you have to maintain it, audit it and explain it, and it contributes nothing.

2. ERP and CRM

Running a SAP module alongside an off-the-shelf system. Two tools with different logic over the same operation — the usual situation, and the most uncomfortable one: you have to decide which is the source of truth for each piece of data, and then hold that decision.

End-to-end inventory management: making system stock and warehouse stock say the same thing. It sounds obvious, and it’s where the credibility of everything else is decided — if inventory lies, no indicator is worth anything.

3. Continuous improvement on the floor

World Class Manufacturing and Lean applied to logistics operations. Standardisation, waste elimination, visual indicators where the work happens.

And something that rarely gets told: training. I built and delivered the sessions that walked people through the processes. A process that only exists in a PDF doesn’t exist — it exists once the person running it understands why it works that way.

Stakeholder management

Management, operations, customers and external auditors all want different things from the same information. Management wants the summary, operations wants actionable detail, the customer wants compliance, and the auditor wants traceability.

Sustaining one system that serves all four — without four parallel systems — was a good part of the job.

Outcome

  • Certification and recertification of all three standards passed.
  • The system gets used: records live where the work happens, not in a binder someone fills in before the audit.
  • [Fill in] what improved in numbers: complaints, inventory shrinkage, picking time, incidents.

What I took from it

That continuous improvement and the management system are the same thing seen from two sides. Managed separately, the system turns into bureaucracy and the improvement turns informal — and neither one holds.
